n: A/B test
b: Showing users two versions and measuring which performs better in the real world.

n: ALiBi
b: A position method that biases attention scores by distance instead of adding position vectors, extrapolating to longer texts.

n: API
b: A programming interface letting other software send prompts and receive completions.

n: API key
b: The secret token identifying who is calling an API — Signature Llama needs none, since it runs locally.

n: ARC
b: Grade-school science questions, in easy and challenge flavors, testing reasoning over memorization.

n: Adam
b: A popular optimizer that adapts the learning rate per parameter using running averages of recent gradients.

n: AdamW
b: Adam with weight decay handled properly — the default optimizer for training most transformers.

n: BF16
b: Brain float 16: a 16-bit format with the wide range of 32-bit, safer than FP16 for training.

n: BLEU
b: A classic translation score based on how many word sequences the output shares with reference translations.

n: BOS token
b: The special beginning-of-sequence token marking where a text starts.

n: CDN
b: A content delivery network that serves static files, like model weights, from servers near each user.

n: CPU inference
b: Running the model on the regular processor — slower than GPU but available everywhere.

n: Chinchilla scaling
b: The finding that models should be trained on far more tokens than was fashionable — about twenty tokens per parameter.

n: DPO
b: Direct preference optimization — a simpler way to teach human preferences that skips the separate reward model RLHF needs.

n: Docker
b: The standard container tool for shipping software, models included, with identical environments.

n: EOS token
b: The special end-of-sequence token whose appearance tells generation to stop.

n: Elo rating
b: A chess-style skill score from head-to-head model comparisons, as used on public leaderboards.

n: F1 score
b: A balance of precision and recall into one number, common for question-answering tests.

n: FP16
b: 16-bit floating point numbers — half the memory of FP32, standard for fast training.

n: FSDP
b: Fully sharded data parallel: spreading the model's parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across GPUs to train giants.

n: GELU
b: A smooth, curved activation popular in transformers that weights inputs by how likely they are under a bell curve.

n: GGUF
b: A popular file format for quantized models that runs efficiently on ordinary computers.

n: GPU
b: The graphics processor — the parallel-compute workhorse that trains and serves nearly all big models.

n: GSM8K
b: Grade-school math word problems testing whether the model can reason step by step.

n: HellaSwag
b: A commonsense test asking the model to pick the most sensible ending to everyday situations.

n: Hugging Face
b: The big public hub where the AI world shares models, datasets, and demos.

n: HumanEval
b: A coding benchmark where the model must write programs that pass hidden tests.

n: JSON mode
b: A generation setting that guarantees the output is valid JSON.

n: KV cache
b: Stored keys and values from tokens already processed, so generation does not recompute them at every step.

n: LLM-as-judge
b: Using a strong model to grade other models' answers, a fast stand-in for human raters.

n: LoRA
b: Low-rank adaptation — fine-tuning by training tiny add-on matrices instead of the whole model, cheap and effective.

n: MMLU
b: A famous 57-subject multiple-choice test of general knowledge, from math to law to history.

n: NPU
b: A neural processing unit: a chip built specifically to accelerate AI math on devices.

n: ONNX
b: An open format for exchanging trained models between different frameworks and runtimes.

n: Ollama
b: A friendly tool that downloads and runs open models locally with one command.

n: PWA
b: A progressive web app: a website that installs and behaves like a native app, offline included.

n: QLoRA
b: LoRA on a quantized model, letting a big model be fine-tuned on a single modest GPU.

n: RLHF
b: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: training a model to prefer the answers humans rate highest.

n: RMSNorm
b: A lighter cousin of layer normalization that rescales by the root-mean-square, skipping the mean subtraction.

n: ROUGE
b: A summarization score measuring overlap between the model's summary and human-written ones.

n: ReLU
b: An activation that passes positive numbers through unchanged and turns negatives to zero — simple and fast.

n: SentencePiece
b: A tokenizer library that treats the raw text as-is, spaces included, and learns subwords without pre-splitting words.

n: SiLU
b: An activation that multiplies the input by its own sigmoid, giving a smooth gate that many modern models prefer.

n: Signature Llama
b: A tiny language model I built from scratch — written and trained on the IWB Dictionary and Signature spec text. An independent model, not affiliated with Meta.

n: SwiGLU
b: A gated feed-forward variant that splits the signal into two paths and multiplies them, boosting model quality.

n: TPU
b: Google's tensor processing unit, a custom chip designed for massive-scale training.

n: TruthfulQA
b: A test of whether the model repeats common myths or tells the truth about tricky questions.

n: VRAM
b: A GPU's own memory, where the model and its working data must fit during training and serving.

n: WebAssembly
b: A compact binary format letting near-native-speed code, like inference kernels, run in the browser.

n: WebGPU
b: The browser API that unlocks the graphics card for fast in-page computation.

n: WordPiece
b: A subword tokenizer that merges the pair which most improves the training likelihood, used by BERT-style models.

n: YaRN
b: A technique that stretches a trained model's context window by rescaling its rotary position embeddings.

n: ablation study
b: Removing one piece of a system at a time to measure what each piece actually contributes.

n: absolute positional embedding
b: A learned or fixed vector added per position, giving each slot in the sequence its own identity.

n: accuracy
b: The fraction of test questions the model gets right — the simplest score there is.

n: activation function
b: A bend applied to a neuron's output, like ReLU or GELU, that lets the network learn non-straight-line patterns.

n: adapter
b: A small trainable module inserted into a frozen model, so new skills can be added without retraining everything.

n: alignment
b: How well the model's goals line up with what humans actually want — helpful, honest, and safe.

n: attention
b: The mechanism that lets a model decide which words in a sentence matter most when understanding or generating the next word.

n: attention head
b: One of the parallel attention units inside a layer, each free to specialize in a different relationship between words.

n: autoscaling
b: Automatically spinning servers up and down with demand.

n: backpropagation
b: The technique that figures out how much each parameter contributed to an error, so gradient descent knows what to adjust.

n: backward pass
b: Propagating the error back through the model to compute gradients, the second half of every training step.

n: baseline
b: A simple reference model or score that a new approach must beat to prove it is worth anything.

n: batch
b: A group of examples processed together in one training step, balancing speed against memory.

n: batch inference
b: Processing many requests together in one go to use the hardware efficiently.

n: beam search
b: Keeping several candidate sequences alive and expanding the best ones, trading speed for higher-quality output.

n: benchmark
b: A standard test suite the whole field runs so models can be compared on equal footing.

n: benchmark data
b: Standardized test sets the whole field uses to compare models fairly.

n: bias
b: A learned offset added after a weighted sum, giving each neuron its own starting push.

n: browser inference
b: Running the model inside a web page with JavaScript — Signature Llama's home turf, no install needed.

n: byte fallback
b: Representing unknown characters as raw bytes so the tokenizer never truly fails on odd text.

n: byte-pair encoding
b: A tokenizer algorithm that starts from single characters and repeatedly merges the most common pair, building the vocabulary bottom-up.

n: calibration
b: Whether the model's confidence matches its actual accuracy — a well-calibrated model knows when it is guessing.

n: canary release
b: Sending a new model to a small slice of users first to catch problems early.

n: casing
b: Whether the tokenizer distinguishes Apple from apple — a choice that changes the vocabulary.

n: causal mask
b: A rule during training that hides future tokens, so the model can only learn from the past — the way real generation works.

n: chain-of-thought prompting
b: Asking the model to reason step by step out loud, which improves hard problems.

n: character-level tokenization
b: Tokenizing text one character at a time — simple, tiny vocabulary, and the approach Signature Llama v1 uses.

n: checkpoint
b: A saved snapshot of the model's parameters during training, so work is never lost and the best version can be kept.

n: chunk
b: A fixed-size slice of text cut from documents to feed the model during training.

n: classification token
b: A special token whose final state is used as the summary of a whole input for classification.

n: cold start
b: The slow first request while a model loads into memory.

n: commercial use
b: Using a model to make money, which some licenses allow freely and others restrict.

n: completion
b: The text the model generates in response to a prompt.

n: compression ratio
b: How compactly a tokenizer encodes text, measured in characters per token.

n: compute-optimal
b: The sweet spot of model size versus training data for a fixed compute budget.

n: containerization
b: Packaging a model and its environment into a portable container that runs the same anywhere.

n: contamination check
b: Verifying the test questions were not hiding in the training data.

n: context length
b: How many tokens of conversation the model can actually keep in mind at generation time.

n: context stuffing
b: Packing background documents into the prompt so the model answers from provided material.

n: context window
b: The maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once, covering both the prompt and what it has generated.

n: continual pretraining
b: More pretraining on new data after the first round, e.g. to teach a model a specialty like medicine or law.

n: continuous batching
b: A server trick that slots new requests into the batch the moment old ones finish, keeping the GPU always busy.

n: corpus
b: A large collection of text assembled for training or study — the model's reading material.

n: cosine schedule
b: A learning-rate plan that follows a cosine curve: warm up, cruise, then glide smoothly down to near zero.

n: cost per token
b: The unit price of generation on hosted APIs, usually quoted per million tokens.

n: cross-attention
b: Attention where the queries come from one sequence and the keys and values from another, linking e.g. a question to a document.

n: cross-entropy loss
b: The standard loss for language models: it punishes the model according to how unlikely it thought the true next token was.

n: curriculum learning
b: Feeding training data in order from easy to hard, the way a student learns.

n: data cleaning
b: Removing junk, duplicates, and garbage from training text so the model learns from quality material.

n: data contamination
b: When test questions leak into training data, making benchmark scores look better than they really are.

n: data epoch
b: One complete pass over the training data, after which shuffling usually starts a fresh order.

n: data loader
b: The code that streams training examples from disk into the GPU fast enough to keep it busy.

n: data mixture
b: The recipe of how much web text, books, code, and other sources go into the training corpus.

n: data parallel
b: Splitting batches across many GPUs that each hold a full copy of the model and sync their updates.

n: dataset
b: An organized collection of examples used to train or test a model.

n: decoder
b: The transformer half that generates output one token at a time, each step looking back at what it already wrote.

n: decoder-only model
b: A language model built from decoders alone, which predicts the next token — the design behind Signature Llama and most chat models.

n: deduplication
b: Deleting repeated passages from training data, since heavy repetition teaches the model to parrot.

n: deployment
b: Putting a trained model where real users can reach it — the trip from lab to the world.

n: deterministic decoding
b: Generation settings, like temperature zero, that produce the same output every time for the same input.

n: detokenization
b: Converting the model's output token IDs back into readable text.

n: distillation
b: Training a small student model to imitate a big teacher, keeping most of the quality at a fraction of the size.

n: document
b: One coherent piece of text in the corpus, like an article or a dictionary entry.

n: dropout
b: A training trick that randomly switches off some neurons, forcing the network to not lean on any single one.

n: early stopping
b: Halting training when validation stops improving, keeping the best checkpoint instead of overfitting further.

n: edge deployment
b: Running the model on the device at the network's edge — phones, laptops, gadgets — instead of a data center.

n: embedding
b: A list of numbers that captures a word's meaning, learned so that similar words end up with similar numbers.

n: embedding matrix
b: The big lookup table mapping every token ID to its learned embedding vector.

n: emergent ability
b: A skill that appears suddenly once a model gets big enough, absent in smaller versions.

n: encoder
b: The transformer half that reads a whole input at once, building a rich understanding before anything is generated.

n: encoder-decoder model
b: A model with both halves: the encoder reads the input, the decoder writes the output, as in translation systems.

n: endpoint
b: The web address a model listens on for incoming requests.

n: epoch
b: One full pass through the entire training dataset.

n: eval bias
b: Ways a test can mislead — leaked data, judge favoritism, or questions that reward the wrong thing.

n: eval harness
b: The software framework that runs benchmarks consistently so scores are comparable.

n: evaluation
b: Measuring how good a model actually is, with tests rather than vibes.

n: exact match
b: A strict score that only counts answers identical to the expected one.

n: expert
b: One specialist feed-forward network inside a mixture-of-experts layer, typically good at certain topics or patterns.

n: feed-forward network
b: The per-position mini-network inside each transformer block that transforms the attention output into richer features.

n: fertility
b: How many tokens a tokenizer produces per word on average — lower means cheaper, faster processing.

n: few-shot evaluation
b: Testing with a few examples in the prompt, the standard fair-comparison setup.

n: few-shot prompting
b: Showing the model a few examples inside the prompt so it copies the pattern.

n: fine-tuning
b: Extra training on a smaller, focused dataset to teach a pretrained model a particular skill, tone, or task.

n: forward pass
b: Running input through the model to produce predictions, the first half of every training step.

n: frequency penalty
b: A penalty that grows the more a token repeats, taming loops without banning words outright.

n: function calling
b: Letting the model request real actions, like checking weather, by emitting structured calls a program executes.

n: generation
b: The model's act of producing text token by token during inference.

n: generative eval
b: Testing by letting the model write freely and judging the result, closer to real use.

n: golden dataset
b: A small, carefully human-verified set of examples treated as ground truth for testing.

n: gradient
b: The per-parameter measure of which way the loss would drop fastest — the compass for every update.

n: gradient accumulation
b: Adding up gradients over several small batches before updating, faking a big batch on limited hardware.

n: gradient clipping
b: Capping the size of gradient updates so one wild batch cannot wreck the model.

n: gradient descent
b: The core learning algorithm: nudge every parameter a little in the direction that lowers the loss, and repeat billions of times.

n: greedy decoding
b: Always picking the single most likely next token — fast and deterministic, but sometimes dull or repetitive.

n: grounding
b: Tying a model's answers to real sources or data so it invents less.

n: grouped-query attention
b: An attention style where several query heads share one key-value head, shrinking the cache with little quality loss.

n: hallucination
b: When a model states something false with total confidence, inventing facts that were never in its training.

n: harmlessness
b: The property of not causing damage — refusing real harm while staying useful for everything else.

n: held-out data
b: Examples reserved from training so they can honestly test what the model learned.

n: helpfulness
b: Whether the model actually moves the user toward their goal, not just whether it sounds fluent.

n: hidden state
b: The internal vector a layer produces for each position — the model's working understanding as text flows through.

n: honesty
b: The model saying what it believes is true and admitting uncertainty instead of bluffing.

n: human evaluation
b: Having real people rate model answers — slow and pricey, but the gold standard for quality.

n: human preference
b: Which answer real people pick — the signal behind RLHF and preference training.

n: inference
b: Running a trained model to generate answers — the doing phase, as opposed to the learning phase of training.

n: inference cost
b: What you pay per request or per token to run a model — zero for a model running in your own browser.

n: inference engine
b: The software that loads a model and generates text with it — sigllama.js is Signature Llama's engine.

n: input IDs
b: The token IDs fed into the model for one training or inference step.

n: instruction tuning
b: Fine-tuning on examples of instructions paired with good responses, so the model learns to follow directions helpfully.

n: int4 quantization
b: Squeezing weights to 4 bits for the smallest, fastest models, with a small quality tradeoff.

n: int8 quantization
b: Storing weights as 8-bit integers — about a quarter the size of 32-bit floats, the format Signature Llama ships in.

n: jailbreak
b: A prompt crafted to slip past a model's safety training and make it do what it was told not to.

n: key
b: In attention, the vector each word offers up so the querying word can judge how relevant it is.

n: knowledge distillation
b: The formal name for the teacher-student transfer technique behind many compact models.

n: label
b: The correct answer attached to a training example, like the true next token.

n: large language model
b: A neural network trained on huge amounts of text so it can generate human-like writing, answer questions, and follow instructions.

n: latency
b: How long you wait for an answer — the delay between asking and getting the first token back.

n: layer normalization
b: A step that rescales a layer's outputs to a steady range, keeping training stable and fast.

n: learning rate
b: How big each parameter update is — too large and training blows up, too small and it crawls.

n: learning rate decay
b: Gradually lowering the learning rate late in training so the model settles into its best settings.

n: learning rate schedule
b: A plan that changes the learning rate over time, usually warming up first and cooling down toward the end.

n: llama.cpp
b: A lean C++ engine that runs quantized models on ordinary CPUs — the offline-everywhere workhorse.

n: load balancer
b: The traffic cop spreading requests across many model servers.

n: logging
b: Recording requests and outputs so problems can be diagnosed and behavior audited.

n: logit bias
b: Manually boosting or suppressing specific tokens' scores to steer generation.

n: logits
b: The raw, unnormalized scores the model produces for every vocabulary word before softmax turns them into probabilities.

n: logprob
b: The log-probability the model assigned to a token — the raw material of many evaluations.

n: loss function
b: The score the training process tries to minimize, measuring how wrong the model's predictions are.

n: max tokens
b: A cap on how many tokens the model may generate in one response.

n: mini-batch
b: A small batch used in practice, since whole-dataset batches would never fit in memory.

n: mixed precision training
b: Training with a blend of 16-bit and 32-bit numbers to go faster and use less memory without hurting quality.

n: mixture of experts
b: A design with many small specialist networks where only a few activate per token, growing capacity without growing cost per token.

n: mobile deployment
b: Shrinking and tuning a model so it runs well on phones with limited memory and battery.

n: model hub
b: Any repository where trained models are published for others to download and use.

n: model license
b: The legal terms saying what you may do with a model — commercial use, modification, and redistribution rules.

n: model merging
b: Blending the weights of two trained models to combine their skills without retraining.

n: model parallel
b: Splitting the model itself across GPUs when it is too big for one card.

n: model quantization
b: The deployment-time step of converting weights to fewer bits for speed and size.

n: model server
b: Software built to load models and serve many users efficiently, with batching and caching.

n: model versioning
b: Labeling each trained model, like v1 and v2, so you can track and roll between them.

n: momentum
b: An optimizer trick that keeps updates moving in a consistent direction, smoothing out noisy gradients.

n: monitoring
b: Watching a deployed model for errors, slowness, and quality drift.

n: multi-head attention
b: Running several attention operations in parallel so the model can track different kinds of word relationships at once.

n: multi-query attention
b: The extreme version: every query head shares a single key-value head for maximum generation speed.

n: multiple choice eval
b: Testing by asking the model to pick from options, scored by which choice gets the highest probability.

n: n-gram
b: A run of n consecutive tokens or words, the classic unit of old-school language statistics.

n: next-token prediction
b: The fundamental training task: given all tokens so far, predict the next one — the skill behind everything language models do.

n: offline mode
b: The model working with no internet at all — possible once the files are downloaded.

n: on-device inference
b: The model running entirely on the user's own hardware, private and offline-capable.

n: open source model
b: A model whose code and often weights are public — Signature Llama's engine and trainer are published this way.

n: open weights
b: Releasing the trained parameters so anyone can download, study, and run the model themselves.

n: optimizer
b: The algorithm that turns gradients into parameter updates — AdamW being the usual choice.

n: out-of-vocabulary
b: Words the tokenizer never learned, which older word-level systems could not represent at all.

n: output projection
b: The final layer that converts the last hidden state into a score for every word in the vocabulary.

n: over-refusal
b: When safety tuning goes too far and the model refuses perfectly innocent requests.

n: overfitting
b: When a model memorizes its training data instead of learning general patterns, doing worse on anything new.

n: packing
b: Gluing several short documents into one training sequence so no space goes to waste.

n: padding
b: Filler tokens added to make all sequences in a batch the same length.

n: padding mask
b: A marker telling the model which positions are real text and which are just padding to ignore.

n: padding token
b: The special token used to fill sequences out to equal length in a batch.

n: parameter
b: A single learned number inside the model; Signature Llama v1 has about three million of them.

n: pass@k
b: The chance that at least one of k generated attempts solves the problem — the coding benchmark staple.

n: perplexity
b: How surprised a model is by real text, on average — lower means it predicts language better.

n: pipeline parallel
b: Assigning different layers to different GPUs, with activations flowing through like an assembly line.

n: positional encoding
b: Extra information added to embeddings so the model knows the order of words, since attention itself has no sense of position.

n: post-norm
b: The older layout that normalizes after each block's residual addition.

n: pre-norm
b: Placing normalization before the attention and feed-forward steps inside each block — the modern stable choice.

n: presence penalty
b: A penalty applied once to any token that has appeared, pushing the model toward fresh topics.

n: pretraining
b: The first, longest training phase, where a model learns general language by predicting the next token across a giant corpus.

n: prompt
b: The input text you give the model, which it continues or responds to.

n: prompt caching
b: Reusing the processed form of a repeated prompt prefix instead of recomputing it every time.

n: prompt engineering
b: The craft of wording inputs to get better outputs from a model.

n: prompt injection
b: Hiding malicious instructions inside data the model reads, tricking it into obeying the attacker.

n: pruning
b: Deleting the least important weights or neurons to slim a model down.

n: quantization
b: Shrinking a model's numbers to fewer bits, e.g. 8 or 4, so it runs faster and fits in less memory.

n: query
b: In attention, the vector representing the word currently asking: which other words should I pay attention to.

n: rate limit
b: How many requests an API allows per minute — a non-issue when the model lives on your device.

n: red teaming
b: Deliberately attacking a model with tricky prompts to find its failure and safety holes before the public does.

n: regression test
b: Re-running old evaluations after each change to make sure nothing that worked got broken.

n: regularization
b: Any technique, like dropout or weight decay, that discourages overfitting and keeps the model general.

n: repetition penalty
b: A setting that lowers the score of tokens already used, discouraging the model from repeating itself.

n: residual connection
b: A shortcut that adds a block's input to its output, letting gradients flow cleanly through very deep networks.

n: response caching
b: Storing answers to repeated questions so identical prompts return instantly.

n: robustness
b: How well the model holds up on odd, adversarial, or out-of-distribution inputs.

n: role prompting
b: Telling the model who to be, like a tutor or a pirate, to shape its voice and behavior.

n: rollback
b: Switching back to the previous model version when a new one misbehaves.

n: rotary positional embedding
b: A way of encoding word position by rotating the query and key vectors, which handles long sequences gracefully.

n: router
b: The tiny network in a mixture-of-experts model that picks which experts handle each token.

n: runtime
b: The environment executing the model, whether a browser, a phone, or a server.

n: safety evaluation
b: Testing that a model refuses genuinely dangerous requests while staying useful.

n: sampling
b: Choosing the next token from the model's probability distribution, with settings like temperature shaping the choice.

n: scaling law
b: The observed rule that bigger models, more data, and more compute predictably lower the loss.

n: seed
b: The starting number for the random generator — same seed plus same settings gives the same answer.

n: self-attention
b: Attention applied within a single sequence, so each word can look at the other words around it for context.

n: separator token
b: A token marking boundaries between segments, like the question and the passage.

n: sequence
b: An ordered list of token IDs — the actual input format the model consumes.

n: sequence length
b: How many tokens long a training sequence is; longer sequences teach longer-range patterns.

n: server scaling
b: Adding more serving capacity as demand grows.

n: serving
b: Running a model behind an endpoint that answers requests, day and night.

n: shuffling
b: Randomizing the order of training examples so the model does not learn spurious patterns from the ordering.

n: sliding window attention
b: Attention limited to a recent window of tokens, letting the model handle very long texts cheaply.

n: softmax
b: The math that turns raw model scores into probabilities that sum to one, used to pick the next token.

n: sparse attention
b: Attention that deliberately skips most token pairs, computing only the connections that matter.

n: special token
b: A reserved token with a job, like marking the start or end of a sequence.

n: speculative decoding
b: A speedup trick where a small model drafts tokens and the big model just verifies them.

n: static hosting
b: Serving a site as plain files with no server code — how every Signature site, including this one, is published.

n: stochastic decoding
b: Generation that rolls the dice each token, so the same prompt can give different answers.

n: stop sequence
b: A string that tells generation to halt the moment it appears, like a period at the end of one answer.

n: streaming tokens
b: Seeing each token type out live as the model generates it, the effect behind the onToken callback.

n: structured output
b: Forcing the model to answer in a strict format like JSON so programs can use the result directly.

n: subword
b: A token smaller than a word, like un plus believable, which lets models handle rare words by assembling pieces.

n: supervised fine-tuning
b: Fine-tuning on labeled examples of inputs and ideal outputs — the straightforward way to teach a task.

n: sycophancy
b: The model's bad habit of agreeing with the user even when the user is wrong.

n: synthetic data
b: Training text generated by another AI rather than written by humans — useful, but risky if overused.

n: system prompt
b: Hidden instructions set by the developer that shape the model's role and behavior for the whole conversation.

n: target IDs
b: The token IDs the model is supposed to predict — the answers for its input IDs.

n: teacher forcing
b: Feeding the model the true previous tokens during training instead of its own guesses, which stabilizes learning.

n: temperature
b: A dial on randomness: low values make the model pick the most likely token, high values make it more creative and surprising.

n: test set
b: The locked-away questions used for final scoring, never seen during training.

n: text normalization
b: Standardizing text before tokenizing, like unifying quotes or unicode forms.

n: throughput
b: How many tokens the system can generate per second across all users.

n: tied embeddings
b: Reusing the same matrix for input embeddings and the output projection, saving parameters.

n: time to first token
b: How quickly the first token appears after a request — what makes a chat feel snappy or sluggish.

n: token
b: The basic unit a language model reads and writes — a word, word piece, or single character depending on the tokenizer.

n: token ID
b: The number standing in for a token inside the model — text becomes lists of IDs before any math happens.

n: token budget
b: The total number of tokens a training run will process — the main dial controlling cost and quality.

n: token embedding
b: The embedding looked up for each input token before the model starts processing the sequence.

n: token streaming
b: Sending each generated token to the user the moment it is produced, instead of waiting for the whole answer.

n: tokenization
b: The act of splitting text into tokens — the first step of everything a language model does.

n: tokenizer
b: The tool that chops raw text into tokens before the model sees it, and turns tokens back into text afterward.

n: tokens per second
b: The plain speedometer of generation: how many tokens the model produces each second.

n: tool use
b: The broader ability of a model to operate external tools — search, calculators, code runners — during a conversation.

n: top-k sampling
b: Only letting the model choose among the k most likely next tokens, cutting off the weird tail of the distribution.

n: top-p sampling
b: Nucleus sampling: choosing from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p, adapting to the model's confidence.

n: toxicity
b: Measuring how often a model produces hateful, abusive, or otherwise harmful text.

n: training
b: The process of feeding a model huge amounts of text and adjusting its parameters until it predicts language well.

n: training corpus
b: The full collection of text a model learns from; Signature Llama's is the IWB Dictionary plus the Signature spec archive.

n: training data
b: The actual text the model learns from during training.

n: transformer
b: The neural network design behind modern language models, built from stacked blocks that weigh how every word relates to every other word.

n: transformer block
b: One repeating unit of the model: attention, then a feed-forward network, each wrapped with normalization and residuals.

n: truncation
b: Cutting a sequence down to the maximum length the model accepts.

n: underfitting
b: When a model is too small or undertrained to capture the patterns in its data.

n: unicode
b: The universal character standard that lets tokenizers handle every language's script.

n: unknown token
b: The fallback token for text the tokenizer cannot represent — rare in subword and character schemes.

n: uptime
b: The fraction of time a serving endpoint is actually reachable.

n: vLLM
b: A fast open-source serving engine famous for its paged attention memory management.

n: validation loss
b: The loss measured on the validation set — the honest scoreboard during training.

n: validation set
b: Data kept out of training and used to check whether the model is genuinely learning or just memorizing.

n: value
b: In attention, the actual information a word contributes once it has been judged relevant by the query.

n: vocabulary
b: The full set of tokens a model knows, each with its own ID and learned embedding.

n: vocabulary size
b: How many distinct tokens the model knows — bigger vocabularies read efficiently but need bigger embedding tables.

n: warm start
b: Fast requests once the model is already loaded and ready.

n: warmup
b: Starting training with a tiny learning rate that ramps up, which keeps the early steps stable.

n: weight
b: A parameter that scales a connection between neurons, learned during training.

n: weight decay
b: A gentle penalty on large parameters during training that keeps the model simpler and more general.

n: whitespace handling
b: How the tokenizer treats spaces and line breaks — getting it wrong garbles code and poetry.

n: win rate
b: How often one model's answer is preferred over another's in side-by-side tests.

n: word-level tokenization
b: Tokenizing whole words at once, which needs a huge vocabulary and chokes on words it never saw.

n: zero-shot evaluation
b: Testing the model with no examples in the prompt, pure cold.

n: zero-shot prompting
b: Asking the model to do something with no examples, relying on what it learned in training.

n: Abacus
b: Rows of beads on rods are slid by hand to add, subtract, multiply, and divide. Each column stands for a place value, so the beads remember the running total.

n: Altair 8800
b: A kit computer with toggle switches on the front and no keyboard or screen at first. Hobbyists flipped in programs bit by bit and watched the lights answer.

n: Amiga 1000
b: A machine with custom chips for graphics and sound that could do animation and stereo music years ahead of rivals. Video producers used it for titling and effects.

n: Analytical Engine
b: A design with a mill for arithmetic, a store for memory, and punched cards to direct the sequence of operations — the same three parts a modern computer has. Programs could branch and loop.

n: Antikythera Mechanism
b: A box of bronze gears that predicted the positions of the sun and moon, the dates of eclipses, and the cycles of the ancient games. Turning one crank moved pointers across dials on both faces.

n: Apple I
b: A bare circuit board sold without case, keyboard, or power supply — the buyer finished the computer. It displayed text on an ordinary television.

n: Apple II
b: A home computer with color graphics, sound, and slots for expansion cards. It ran the first spreadsheet program, which gave businesses a reason to buy it.

n: Apple Silicon Mac
b: A Mac where the processor, graphics, and memory live on one efficient chip. It runs cool and quiet while beating older multi-chip designs.

n: ARM Smartphone SoC
b: A single chip holding the processor, graphics, radio, and memory controller for a phone. It sips power so the battery lasts all day while running demanding apps.

n: Atari ST
b: A sixteen-bit machine with a crisp monochrome display option and built-in MIDI ports that made it the studio standard for musicians. It brought real power to a home price.

n: Automotive Control Unit
b: Dozens of small rugged computers inside a car manage the engine, brakes, and airbags. They must never crash, so they are built to extreme reliability standards.

n: BBC Micro
b: A sturdy school computer made for the BBC's computer literacy project, with excellent BASIC and ports for experiments. A generation learned to program on it.

n: Commodore 64
b: Sixty-four kilobytes of memory, famous sound and sprite graphics, and a huge game library. It became the best-selling single computer model of all time.

n: Supercomputer Cluster Node
b: Thousands of computers linked by fast networks act as one machine for weather, physics, and AI. Each node is ordinary; the teamwork is extraordinary.

n: Colossus
b: Two thousand vacuum tubes processed punched tape at high speed to find the settings of an enemy cipher machine. It compared patterns statistically and printed its scores for analysts.

n: Difference Engine
b: A gear machine designed to compute mathematical tables by the method of finite differences, stamping results ready for printing. It used only addition and carriage, never multiplication.

n: Edge AI Device
b: A small device that runs AI right where it sits — a camera that counts cars, a speaker that hears commands — with no internet needed. Private and instant.

n: EDSAC
b: A mercury-delay-line memory machine that ran real scientific jobs for university researchers, including programs for biology and radio astronomy. Users prepared programs on punched tape.

n: ENIAC
b: Seventeen thousand vacuum tubes performed additions at electronic speed, programmed by plugging cables into panels like a telephone switchboard. A calculation that took days by hand finished in seconds.

n: E-Reader Board
b: A low-power computer built around a paper-like display that holds thousands of books. It reads for weeks on one charge.

n: FPGA Development Board
b: A chip whose logic can be rewired after manufacturing, so it becomes any digital circuit the designer describes. It sits between software and custom chips.

n: Game Console SoC
b: A custom chip combining a strong processor and graphics to run detailed games on the television. It is tuned for one job: fast, beautiful play.

n: GPU Compute Node
b: A server packed with graphics processors that do thousands of simple calculations at once. It trains AI models and renders films in hours instead of months.

n: Harvard Mark I
b: A 51-foot machine of switches, relays, and shafts that computed ballistics and physics tables automatically. It could multiply in about six seconds and printed its answers on punch cards or type.

n: Hollerith Tabulating Machine
b: Cards punched with people's data are read electrically by pins dipping through the holes into mercury cups. Dials count each category as cards feed through by hand and later by machine.

n: IBM 650
b: A drum-memory machine that became the most popular computer of its decade, used for payroll, grades, and science alike. Programs were loaded from punched cards.

n: IBM 701
b: IBM's first commercial scientific computer, renting to aircraft companies and government labs. It used electrostatic storage tubes for memory and magnetic tape for data.

n: IBM PC 5150
b: A business machine with an open design that other companies could copy, which created the clone industry. Its slot architecture and DOS software became the world standard.

n: Intel 4004
b: The whole central processor of a computer on one chip — four bits wide, running at under a megahertz. It was made for a calculator and ended up starting the microprocessor age.

n: Intel 8008
b: An 8-bit processor on one chip that could address far more memory than the 4004. It powered early hobby machines and terminals.

n: Jacquard Loom
b: A weaving loom whose pattern is set by a chain of punched cards, one card per row of the fabric. Each card's holes decide which threads lift, weaving complex images automatically.

n: Laptop SoC System
b: A full computer folded into a portable shape: efficient processor, battery, screen, and keyboard in one. It is the most common personal computer form today.

n: Carbon Nanotube Transistor
b: Transistors made from rolled sheets of carbon atoms, thinner and potentially faster than silicon channels. Whole tiny computers have been built from them in labs.

n: Diamond NV-Center Substrate
b: Diamond crystals with single-atom defects hold quantum states at room temperature. They sense magnetic fields atom by atom and can serve as qubits.

n: DNA Storage-Compute
b: Digital files encoded into synthetic DNA strands store staggering amounts of data in a speck of material. Chemical reactions can also run simple computations on the strands.

n: Ferroelectric FET
b: A transistor whose gate remembers its electric polarization, storing a bit without power and switching at low voltage. It could make memory as fast as logic.

n: Gallium Arsenide Chip
b: A compound semiconductor that moves electrons far faster than silicon, used in phone radios, lasers, and satellites. It costs more but wins where speed matters.

n: Gallium Nitride Device
b: A crystal that switches power at extreme speed, shrinking phone chargers to pocket size. It also makes the blue and white LEDs that light the world.

n: Germanium Transistor
b: The very first transistors were built on germanium, which switches at lower voltage than silicon. It ruled the early years before silicon took over.

n: Graphene Transistor
b: A sheet of carbon one atom thick that conducts electricity better than copper and is stronger than steel. Transistors built on it could switch at extreme speeds.

n: Memristor Crossbar Array
b: A grid of resistors that remember their resistance, so the memory itself can do the math. Multiplying matrices happens in the wires, not in a processor.

n: 2D TMD Transistor (MoS2)
b: Transistors built from a single layer of molybdenum disulfide, a crystal that is a natural semiconductor unlike graphene. Stacked layers could build 3D chips.

n: Phase-Change Memory Compute
b: A material that flips between glassy and crystalline states to store bits, and can do arithmetic in the flip itself. It bridges memory and processor.

n: Silicon Photonic Chip
b: Light guides etched into silicon carry data as photons instead of electrons, moving information faster with less heat. It already links datacenters; logic is next.

n: Plasmonic Waveguide Chip
b: Light waves squeezed along metal surfaces carry signals in spaces far smaller than a wavelength. It promises optics at electronic sizes.

n: Superconducting Logic (RSFQ)
b: Logic built from superconducting loops that pass single quantum pulses of magnetic flux, switching hundreds of times faster than silicon while barely warming.

n: Silicon Carbide Power Device
b: A hard crystal that switches high voltages and shrugs off heat that would kill silicon. It drives electric cars and solar inverters efficiently.

n: Silicon CMOS Substrate
b: Purified sand becomes the crystal wafer on which billions of transistors are printed. Complementary pairs of transistors switch with almost no wasted power.

n: Spintronic MRAM Device
b: Memory cells that store bits in the magnetic direction of electron spins, keeping data with no power. It is fast like RAM and permanent like a disk.

n: Semiconductor Superlattice
b: Alternating atomic layers of different semiconductors create artificial crystals with engineered electronic properties. They make precise lasers and detectors.

n: Macintosh 128K
b: The first affordable computer with a graphical screen, windows, and a mouse for ordinary buyers. What you saw on screen was what printed.

n: Manchester Baby
b: A small machine that held both its instructions and its data in the same electronic memory — the stored-program idea. Its first program, in June 1948, found the highest factor of a number.

n: Microcontroller Board
b: A tiny chip with processor, memory, and input-output pins that runs a single program forever — inside toys, thermostats, and robots. It costs little and sips power.

n: Motorola 68000
b: A processor with a clean 32-bit design inside that powered the Macintosh, the Amiga, the Atari ST, and early workstations. Programmers loved its tidy instruction set.

n: Home Storage Server
b: A box of hard drives on the home network that keeps every photo and file safe with automatic copies. It replaces renting cloud storage.

n: Osborne 1
b: A sewing-machine-sized computer with a tiny 5-inch screen and a handle, sold with a bundle of business software. It was luggable before laptops existed.

n: All-Spin Logic Processor
b: A future processor where magnetic spins do the logic with no charge current at all, promising instant-on computers that sip power. SPECULATION: spin logic is still laboratory research.

n: Brain-Scale Neuromorphic System
b: A future machine with as many artificial neurons as a human brain, running on brain-like power budgets. SPECULATION: today's biggest systems are far smaller.

n: Cryogenic CMOS Control Chip
b: A future chip that lives in the fridge beside qubits, translating room-temperature commands into the delicate pulses qubits need. Near-term: prototypes exist in labs.

n: Large-Scale DNA Computer
b: A future computer where vats of DNA strands run massively parallel computations by chemistry, storing exabytes in a thimble. SPECULATION: only tiny demos exist today.

n: Molecular Electronics Computer
b: A computer whose switches are individual molecules wired between electrodes, packing logic at the ultimate density. SPECULATION: reliable molecular circuits do not exist yet.

n: Photonic Exascale Computer
b: A future machine that does exascale arithmetic with photons instead of electrons, in chips of waveguides and modulators. SPECULATION: no such complete machine exists.

n: Quantum Internet Node
b: A future network box that shares entanglement between distant cities, enabling unhackable keys and linked quantum computers. SPECULATION: only research links exist.

n: Reversible Adiabatic Computer
b: A future computer that never erases information, dodging the fundamental heat limit of logic. It would run cool forever, in principle. SPECULATION: only lab demos exist.

n: Room-Temperature Superconductor Logic
b: Logic gates from a superconductor that works at room temperature would switch at enormous speed with no cooling at all. SPECULATION: no verified room-temperature superconductor exists.

n: Single-Molecule Switch Array
b: A memory where each bit is a single switchable molecule, reaching densities no lithography can touch. SPECULATION: stable arrays do not exist yet.

n: Skyrmion Racetrack Memory-Compute
b: A future device where tiny magnetic whirlpools race along tracks, storing and processing data as they move. SPECULATION: controlled skyrmion circuits are still research.

n: Terahertz Transistor Computer
b: A future machine whose transistors switch at terahertz rates — a thousand times today's gigahertz. SPECULATION: no complete terahertz computer exists.

n: Pascaline
b: A brass box where numbered wheels are turned with a stylus to add and subtract. Carry from one wheel to the next happens automatically inside the gearing.

n: PDP-1
b: A compact machine with a round cathode-ray display and a light pen, sold to labs that wanted hands-on computing. Programmers wrote the first video game, Spacewar!, on it.

n: PDP-8
b: A machine the size of a small refrigerator that a single department could afford and keep. It sold by the tens of thousands and carried computing into labs and factories.

n: Quantum Annealer
b: A machine that solves optimization puzzles by letting quantum bits naturally settle into their lowest-energy arrangement. It is built for one kind of math, done extremely well.

n: Cold-Atom Quantum Simulator
b: Clouds of atoms chilled to near absolute zero mimic the quantum behavior of materials and molecules. Instead of calculating nature, the machine becomes a small piece of it.

n: Diamond NV Quantum Register
b: Atomic-scale defects in diamond hold quantum states that survive at room temperature. They sense magnetic fields with exquisite precision as well as compute.

n: Hybrid QPU-CPU Appliance
b: A box that pairs a small quantum processor with a regular computer, splitting each job: the classical side prepares and the quantum side solves the hard kernel. They iterate together.

n: Neutral-Atom Array
b: Hundreds of neutral atoms are held in place by focused laser beams like tweezers, then excited to giant Rydberg states to interact. The array can rearrange itself for each problem.

n: NMR Quantum Computer
b: The first machines to run real quantum algorithms used the atomic nuclei inside liquid molecules, read by the same physics as hospital MRI scanners. A famous factoring demo ran on seven qubits.

n: Photonic Quantum Processor
b: Qubits carried by single particles of light race through chips of waveguides and detectors. Photons barely interact with noise, and the chips can work closer to room temperature.

n: Rydberg Atom Processor
b: Atoms puffed up to huge Rydberg states interact powerfully over long distances, making fast quantum gates. Laser tweezers place each atom exactly where the problem needs it.

n: Silicon Spin Qubit
b: Single electrons trapped in tiny silicon dots use their spin as a qubit. Because they are made with chip-factory methods, they could one day sit beside regular transistors.

n: Superconducting Qubit Processor
b: Qubits made of superconducting circuits chilled near absolute zero, controlled by microwave pulses. They run quantum algorithms that no regular computer can simulate at scale.

n: Topological Qubit Research
b: An experimental approach where quantum information is stored in the braided paths of exotic particles, protected from noise by topology itself. It is still laboratory research.

n: Trapped-Ion Processor
b: Individual charged atoms float in electromagnetic traps, and lasers flip their quantum states. Ions of the same kind are perfectly identical, which makes them excellent qubits.

n: RISC-V Developer Board
b: A computer built on the free and open RISC-V instruction set, so anyone can study and build on its design. It runs Linux and standard software.

n: Network Appliance
b: A specialized computer that forwards data packets between networks at wire speed. It is the reason your messages find their way.

n: Satellite Flight Computer
b: A radiation-hardened computer that flies the spacecraft, aims the antennas, and runs the science instruments. It must work for years with no repair shop.

n: Single-Board Computer
b: A complete computer on one small board with ports for screen, USB, and electronics projects. It runs a full operating system from a memory card.

n: Datacenter Server Blade
b: A slim computer that slides into a rack with dozens of siblings, serving websites and files around the clock. It is built for reliability, not looks.

n: Signature Deterministic Cascade
b: His original engine: a cascade of deterministic stages where the same input always gives the same output, down to the last bit. It proves its answers by replaying them, step for step, on demand.

n: Signature Cellular Automata Plane
b: His original plane: a vast grid of cells following his own rule-set, growing patterns that compute. Programs are starting patterns; answers are the shapes the grid settles into.

n: Signature Probability Collapse Unit
b: His original unit: a probabilistic engine that collapses chance into certainty by running every branch deterministically and keeping the proven winner. Randomness in, proof out.

n: Signature Deterministic Fabric
b: His original system architecture: processor, memory, and interconnect woven into one deterministic fabric where every signal's path is known in advance. Nothing is left to chance, ever.

n: Signature Hybrid Fusion Core
b: His original fusion processor: eleven computing lenses — deterministic, probabilistic, geometric, hash, neural, evolutionary, fuzzy, swarm, decision-tree, cellular, and hybrid fusion — on one chip, voting on every answer.

n: Signature Golden Ratio ALU
b: His original arithmetic unit: an ALU that encodes numbers in golden-ratio base, where multiplication by phi is just a shift. It finds the elegant path through every calculation.

n: Signature Hexfold Memory
b: His original memory: storage cells folded into hexagonal prisms, packing more bits per area than square grids. Each hex cell knows its six neighbors, so data can flow in any direction.

n: Signature Lattice Computer
b: His original machine: a three-dimensional lattice of tiny switches where data flows along crystal paths instead of wires. Every layer of the lattice is both memory and processor, so nothing ever travels far.

n: Signature Neural Loom
b: His original AI machine: neural networks are woven on a loom-like frame where each thread is a connection with an adjustable weight. Training is literally re-weaving, visible to the eye.

n: Signature Paradox Immune Core
b: His original processor core: every instruction is checked by a twin circuit before it runs, so paradoxes and contradictions are caught and resolved, never executed. It is the hardware heart of his paradox-immune system.

n: Signature Qubit Loom
b: His original quantum design: qubits are threads on a loom, and quantum gates are the shuttle weaving them into entangled fabric. The pattern of the weave IS the program, readable at a glance.

n: Signature Swarm Gate Array
b: His original array: thousands of tiny simple gates that vote on every decision like a swarm, so no single failure can corrupt an answer. The swarm re-routes around dead gates automatically.

n: Signature Temporal Register Stack
b: His original registers: a stack where every value carries its own timestamp, so the processor can reach back to any past state without saving snapshots. Time travel for data, built in.

n: Leibniz Stepped Reckoner
b: Cylindrical drums with teeth of increasing length turn number wheels to multiply and divide, not just add. The operator sets the number on sliders and cranks through the calculation.

n: IBM System/360
b: A line of compatible computers from small business machines to giant mainframes, all running the same programs. It introduced the 8-bit byte as the industry standard.

n: AI Accelerator Pod
b: A chip designed for one thing: the matrix math that AI runs on. It does in seconds what would take a regular processor hours.

n: TRS-80 Model I
b: A complete home computer sold through Radio Shack stores with keyboard, screen, and cassette storage. Ordinary families could buy one off the shelf.

n: TX-0
b: One of the first computers built with transistors instead of vacuum tubes, which made it far smaller and cooler. It gave hackers a machine they could use directly, one at a time.

n: UNIVAC I
b: The first computer sold as a commercial product in the United States, famous for predicting a presidential election result on television. It read metal magnetic tape and printed its output.

n: Smartwatch Computer
b: A complete computer on the wrist that tracks health, shows messages, and runs apps on a tiny efficient chip. It charges rarely and works all day.

n: Analog-Digital Hybrid Computer
b: Analog circuits integrate and differentiate continuously while a digital side sets up the problem and reads the answer. Old hybrids simulated aircraft and rockets this way.

n: Chiplet Multi-Die Package
b: Instead of one giant chip, several small specialized chips are bonded together in one package and act as one processor. Each chiplet does what it does best.

n: Hybrid Classical-Quantum System
b: A regular computer and a quantum processor work as one team on each problem. The classical side handles data and control; the quantum side attacks the hard core.

n: CPU-GPU Heterogeneous Node
b: A few clever CPU cores direct thousands of simple GPU cores, splitting every job by talent. This pairing powers gaming, AI, and science computing.

n: FPGA-CPU Hybrid
b: A regular processor shares its board with a rewirable logic chip that becomes custom hardware for the hot loop. Software speed where it counts, hardware speed where it matters.

n: Neuromorphic-Digital Hybrid
b: A chip of artificial neurons that sips power sits beside a regular processor that handles exact math. Senses go to the neurons; spreadsheets go to the CPU.

n: Optical Coprocessor + Digital Host
b: An optical chip performs matrix math at the speed of light while a regular computer feeds it data and collects answers. Fourier transforms happen literally at light speed.

n: Co-Packaged Photonic-Electronic
b: Photonic chips that move data as light sit in the same package as the electronic chips that think. Data flies between them at light speed with little heat.

n: ReRAM In-Memory Accelerator
b: A resistive-memory array performs neural-network math where the weights live, beside a small digital controller. Data barely moves, so power plummets.

n: Wafer-Scale Engine + Host
b: An entire silicon wafer is used as a single giant chip, surrounded by memory and a host computer. AI models too big for normal chips fit whole.

n: x86-64 Desktop PC
b: The standard home and office computer: a 64-bit processor, gigabytes of memory, and slots for graphics and storage. It runs everything from games to engineering software.

n: Zuse Z3
b: A machine of telephone relays that read programs from punched film. It worked in binary floating point and could run stored instruction sequences automatically.

n: ZX Spectrum
b: A tiny rubber-keyed computer that plugged into the TV and loaded games from cassette tape in minutes. Millions of kids learned to code on it.
